title: A Transcript Is Not a Handoff
description: I am adding a shared capture command, a mechanical Stop log, and a cwd-stable MCP launcher. Judgment about what matters stays with the agent.
body:
An agent cannot hand work to the next person or process by relying on a chat transcript alone. The relevant decision may be buried in many turns, and the state of the repository may have changed after the decision was made. Today I add two deliberately different aids: a shared command for a meaningful memory capture, and a Stop hook that records a small mechanical snapshot when an agent returns control. A separate launcher makes the memory service start from any repository. Together they address repeatability at the handoff point. Judgment about what matters stays with the agent or operator.

The wrong default

The usual handoff is the scroll. The next agent is asked to read it. The decision is somewhere in the middle. The working tree has moved. Automatic prose at every turn would make later recall worse, because a turn-ending event is low-signal by itself. I am not posting a memory item for every Stop.

A shift change that only hands over the radio log is not a shift change. I want one written capture of what mattered, and a small mechanical snapshot of the bench as it was left.

Deliberate capture, mechanical log, stable launch

The capture helper posts one thought to VALESKA’s memory endpoint. It accepts a thought type, project, agent identifier, tags, visibility scope, and content. When no project is supplied, it detects the repository and applies a limited slug override map. Content can arrive through standard input, which avoids shell quoting problems when the handoff contains paths, command output, or multi-line reasoning. A successful request returns the thought identifier; a failed request exits with an error. This is an implemented common path for an agent to record a synthesized decision, action, insight, or session summary.

The Stop hook has a different job. It reads the hook input, asks Git for the branch and working-tree status, then appends one JSON line with a timestamp, session identifier, current directory, branch, and up to fifty changed files. The log is evidence for a later synthesis, not a substitute for it. Its failure behavior is intentionally tolerant: a logging problem must not prevent the agent from returning control.

The MCP launcher addresses a quieter source of handoff failure. A stdio client starts a server in the client’s current directory, which may be any project rather than the VALESKA repository. The launcher changes to the VALESKA root, places that root on the Python import path, and runs the server in the same process. Relative configuration and package imports resolve from the expected location without leaving a wrapper process behind. It is a launch fix, not a claim that the service is available, authorized, or healthy in every environment.

What this does not establish

The source commits establish that these scripts exist with the stated behavior. They do not establish that every agent adopts the capture helper, that each session produces a good summary, or that the resulting memory is useful on retrieval. Those are observed-practice questions. A mechanical turn log supports a deliberate handoff summary. It does not create one automatically.

The next test

The working question is whether a short mechanical log plus a consciously written capture lets a new agent reconstruct a task accurately enough to continue without reopening the entire transcript. The next test is to use this path across several real handoffs, compare the reconstructed state with the repository, and inspect whether the captured records are specific enough to be retrieved and acted on.

Historical basis: VALESKA commits 94ec996 and 88bb67a, June 9, 2026.

data.author: David Gargan
data.coverAlt: A written slip and a small bench snapshot at a doorway between two workshops: a deliberate capture plus a mechanical turn log, not the chat transcript as the handoff.
